elements.id-string-12: In this review, we focus on whether a canonical quantization of general relativity can produce testable predictions for cosmology.
elements.id-string-13: In particular, we examine how this approach can be used to model the evolution of primordial perturbations.
elements.id-string-14: This program of quantum geometrodynamics, first advocated by John Wheeler and Bryce DeWitt, has a straightforward classical limit, and it describes the quantum dynamics of all fields, gravitational and matter.
elements.id-string-15: In this context, in which a classical background metric is absent, it is necessary to discuss what constitutes an observation.
elements.id-string-16: We first address this issue in the classical theory and then turn to the quantum theory.
elements.id-string-17: We argue that predictions are relational, that is, relative to physical clocks and rods, and that they can be straightforwardly obtained in a perturbative approach with respect to Newton's constant, which serves as a coupling parameter.
elements.id-string-18: This weak-coupling expansion leads to a perturbative Hilbert space for quantum cosmology, and to corrections to the dynamics of quantum fields on a classical, fixed background metric.
elements.id-string-19: These corrections imply modifications of primordial power spectra, which may lead to signatures in the anisotropy spectrum of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation, for which we discuss concrete results.
elements.id-string-20: We conclude that the subject of quantum geometrodynamics, the oldest and most conservative approach to canonical quantum gravity, not only illuminates conceptual issues in quantum gravitation, but may also lead to observational prospects in cosmology and elsewhere.

elements.id-string-31: From conservative extensions of quantum field theory and gravitation to more imaginative approaches, all of them ultimately seek to unravel the mystery of how quantum mechanics and general relativity might come together to explain the origin and evolution of the Cosmos.
elements.id-string-32: Far from being a collection of mathematical curiosities, the results obtained so far offer us suggestions of experimental tests, as well as hints of the limits of applicability of the formalisms.

elements.id-string-180: \subsection{What is an observation in classical geometrodynamics?}
elements.id-string-181: Before we proceed to discuss observations in quantum cosmology, it is instructive to consider what constitutes an observation in the classical setting.
elements.id-string-182: What can we observe in GR?
elements.id-string-183: The concept of observability of an entity can generally entail two notions: that of its measurability (which concerns its value at a spacetime point), and that of its predictability (which concerns its variations across spacetime, or an estimation of its value in a region $\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{M}$ given the knowledge of its value in another region $\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{M}$).
elements.id-string-184: It seems uncontroversial to assume that tensor fields and other geometric quantities or, more generally, functionals of the fields $g_{\mu\nu}, p^{ab}, \phi$ and $p_{\phi}$ can be, in principle, measured by a suitable apparatus.
elements.id-string-185: Thus, if observability is simply defined to be synonymous with measurability, then general geometric objects such as tensor fields are likely to be observable.
elements.id-string-186: But not all such entities are predictable.
elements.id-string-187: This is the reason why the terminology `partial observable' is sometimes assigned to a measurable but not predictable quantity \citep{Rovelli:2001bz}.
